lines.text: Athena appeared to him and told him what was waiting at his house.
He'd been gone twenty years, ten at the war and ten at sea, and everyone believed he was dead.
So more than a hundred young men from the islands had moved into his palace to court his wife, Penelope.
They ate his cattle and drank his wine, they slept with his servant girls,
and every single day they demanded that she pick one of them to marry.
For years she'd tricked them.
She told them she'd choose a husband once she finished weaving a burial shroud for Odysseus's old father.
She worked on it every day, and every night, in secret, she unpicked what she'd woven.
It worked for three years, until one of her maids gave her away.
His son, Telemachus, had been a baby when Odysseus sailed for Troy.
Now he was a grown man, and the suitors were planning to murder him.
Athena touched Odysseus with her wand.
His skin wrinkled, his hair fell out, and his eyes went cloudy, and she dressed him in filthy rags so that nobody would know him.
He walked into his own town as a beggar.
At the gate of the palace, lying on a heap of dung, was an old dog, crawling with fleas and too weak to stand.
It was Argos.
Odysseus had raised him from a puppy, just before he left for Troy.
After twenty years, not one person had recognised Odysseus.
The dog knew him at once.
He flattened his ears and wagged his tail, but he couldn't get up to go to him.
And Odysseus couldn't go to the dog without giving himself away.
So he walked past, and wiped away a tear before anyone could see it.
And Argos, having seen his master again after twenty years, died.
Inside, the suitors made fun of the beggar.
One threw a stool at him, another a footstool, another a cow's hoof.
Odysseus took all of it without a word, and he watched them.
That night Penelope sat down to talk with the stranger, with no idea who he was, and told him what she'd decided.
Tomorrow, she said, I'll bring out my husband's bow.
Whoever can string it and shoot an arrow through twelve axe heads in a row, the way Odysseus used to, I'll marry him.
The next day the suitors tried, one after another.
They warmed the bow by the fire and rubbed it with fat to soften it, and not one of them could even bend it.
Then the beggar asked for a turn.
They laughed at him, and they shouted.
But Telemachus handed him the bow.
Odysseus turned it over in his hands, the way a musician picks up a lyre he knows.
Then, without even getting up from his seat, he strung it, easily.
He plucked the string, and it sang like a swallow.
Out of a clear sky, Zeus thundered.
He fitted an arrow, and shot it through all twelve axes without touching one.
Then he tore off his rags, leapt onto the threshold, and poured the arrows out at his feet.
The first one went into the throat of Antinous, the leader of the suitors, just as he was lifting a cup of wine to his mouth.
You dogs, said Odysseus. You thought I'd never come home.
The doors were locked, and the spears had been taken down off the walls the night before.
Odysseus, his son, and two servants who'd stayed loyal fought more than a hundred men in that hall,
and they kept fighting until the floor ran with blood and nobody else was left standing.
The old nurse ran upstairs to wake Penelope.
He's here, she told her. Odysseus is home, and he's killed them all.
Penelope came down and sat across the fire from him, and looked at him for a long time, and said nothing.
Telemachus was furious with her. Mother, he said, how can you be so cold?
But she'd waited twenty years, and in that time gods had walked through her house in disguise.
She wasn't going to throw her arms around a stranger because he said he was her husband.
So she tested him. She turned to the nurse and said: move our bed out of the bedroom so he can sleep on it.
And Odysseus, the man who'd tricked a giant and a witch and a hundred suitors, finally lost his temper.
Who moved my bed? Nobody can move that bed.
I built it myself, around the trunk of an olive tree that was growing right there in the house.
The tree is one of its legs. To move it, you'd have to cut it down.
Only the two of them had ever known that.
Penelope ran to him then, and held him, and cried.
He'd set out with twelve ships and six hundred men, and he'd lost every one of them along the way,
some to the sea and the monsters, some to the gods, and more than a few to his own pride.
But he was home.
And that night, Athena held back the dawn, so the night would last a little longer.
